title: Under the Floorboards

post.author: u/hollinmere_stove
post.title: I'm the night warden at a grief retreat. Our guests burn their letters on their last night. One guest's burned letter is back in her journal, dated before the night she burned it.

blocks.text: Hollinmere is a grief retreat in an old farmhouse. Guests stay three weeks. In our journal app they write letters to the people they have lost, and on their last night they burn them: the Burn button deletes the letter while we light a candle in the yard. I'm the night warden. I keep the stove in, lock the doors, and look after the three little computers that hold the journal: one in the main house, one in the barn, and one in the crawl space under the cottage floorboards, down among the old stone foundations. Ingleby, who looks after our computers on Saturdays, says each one keeps a whole copy, so we can lose one.
On 3 February at 09:00 storm water got into the crawl space. We switched the cottage computer off and lifted the floor to dry the stones. It stayed off for 12 days.

On 4 February at 22:10 Isaura burned her letter to her mother. She had written it on 1 February at 21:15, and it was 2,312 bytes; she asked me how long it was, and I looked. The app said Burned. The candle went out by itself. She went home in the morning.

On 15 February at 09:00 we put the floor back and switched the cottage on. On Monday 16 February, at breakfast, Isaura emailed me. Her letter was back in her journal, dated 1 February. Every word where she left it.
Ingleby printed what the computers wrote down:

04 Feb 22:10  house    DELETE letter (QUORUM)   tombstone written
04 Feb 22:10  barn     DELETE letter (QUORUM)   tombstone written
04 Feb 22:10  cottage  unreachable, no hint kept
15 Feb 03:00  house    full compaction   letter 01 Feb 21:15 + tombstone 04 Feb 22:10   both dropped
15 Feb 03:00  barn     full compaction   letter 01 Feb 21:15 + tombstone 04 Feb 22:10   both dropped
15 Feb 09:00  cottage  node up after 12 days
16 Feb 02:00  repair   cottage: letter 01 Feb 21:15   house: none   barn: none   streamed to house, barn
Two of the computers agreed she had burned it. Then the one under the floor remembered it, and now all three do.
Ingleby says nothing is broken; every computer reports healthy. The owner wants to buy two more, so one forgetful copy is always outvoted. What do we change before the next storm?

blocks.label: ingleby_letter_timeline.png
blocks.caption: Ingleby's printout, drawn. The cottage was off from 3 to 15 February. The house and the barn each wrote a tombstone at 22:10 on 4 February, and both dropped the letter and its tombstone at 03:00 on 15 February. The cottage came back at 09:00 with the only copy, and the repair at 02:00 on 16 February streamed it to the other two.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your journal runs on Cassandra, which never edits a data file once it's written. Those files are SSTables: sorted files on disk, written once and only read after. So a delete can't rub the letter out. It writes a tombstone instead, a small marker that says "deleted at 22:10 on 4 February", into a newer file. Compaction is the cleanup that later merges files, keeps the newest version of each thing and drops what's hidden. A tombstone itself may be dropped once it's older than the table's gc_grace_seconds, its grace period. And while a node is off, the others keep hints, notes of the writes it missed, but only for the first max_hint_window of the outage. Now Ingleby's printout. On 15 February at 03:00, how old was the tombstone, and what was the grace? Where was the cottage then? When the repair compared three copies on the 16th, what did the house and the barn have to set against the cottage's letter? And when had the cottage last been part of a repair?

replies.author: u/hollinmere_stove
replies.text: Ingleby read me the settings: max_hint_window is 3h, and gc_grace_seconds on the letters table is 864000. The repair runs by itself every Monday at 02:00. On 9 February it ran on the house and the barn only; the cottage was off. The cottage came back six hours after the merge.

comments.author: u/clean_hearth_vosper
comments.text: Tombstones are clutter. Every one is a deleted thing your disks keep carrying, and Cassandra reads get slower as they pile up. Set gc_grace_seconds to 0 and a burned letter leaves the disk at the next compaction, which is what burned should mean. Ten days of keeping a deleted letter around is ten days of a promise not kept. I run my tables with a short grace and sleep fine.

comments.author: u/locked_drawer_trelawney
comments.text: Don't delete at all. Add a burned column, set it to true, and have the app hide burned letters. An update with a newer timestamp can't be outvoted by an old copy, there's no tombstone to lose, and if a guest regrets it you can undo it. My team stopped deleting rows years ago.

reply.prompt: The storms come every winter, and the cottage floor will be lifted again. What should Hollinmere change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Set gc_grace_seconds to 0, so a burned letter and its tombstone leave every disk at the next compaction.
options.part2: Ingleby set gc_grace_seconds to 0 on the letters table. The next winter the crawl space flooded again, and the cottage computer was off for 12 days. On the second night a guest burned her letter, and the house and the barn wrote tombstones. The nightly compactions didn't drop them, even at a grace of zero: the letter's old SSTable was never in those merges, and a tombstone can't go while an older copy of the row sits outside the merge. On the twelfth day at 03:00 the full compaction merged everything, and the letter and its tombstone went together, on the same day they had gone in February. The cottage came back at 09:00 holding the letter, and the Monday repair at 02:00 streamed it to the other two. Her letter was back on the same schedule as Isaura's. The disks were a little emptier, and the cottage didn't care.
options.senior: A grace of zero doesn't carry a delete to a replica that was off; it only removes the time repair had to carry it there. At Hollinmere the letter and its tombstone first met in one merge on the twelfth day either way, so the letter came back on the same day. With any outage that spans a merge, a zero grace loses a missed delete the moment the merge runs. Keep the grace longer than your repair interval plus slack, and cut tombstone cost elsewhere.

options.text: Buy two more nodes and raise the replication factor to 5, so a single forgetful copy is always outvoted.
options.part2: The owner bought two more computers, one for the dairy and one for the stable, and Ingleby raised the replication factor to 5. The next winter the cottage was off for 12 days again. On the second night a guest burned her letter. The DELETE at QUORUM, now 3 of 5, reached the house, the barn, the dairy and the stable, and all four wrote tombstones. On the twelfth day at 03:00 the full compaction dropped the letter and its tombstone on all four. The cottage came back at 09:00 with the only copy, and the Monday repair streamed it to all four. Four empty copies didn't outvote one full one; nothing was counted at all. Her letter came back five times over: 11,560 bytes on disk instead of 6,936.
options.senior: Repair and reads don't count heads for deleted. Once the tombstones are gone, the other replicas hold nothing, and nothing loses to any value: an absent row is not a vote. More replicas survive more node losses, but every replica must still receive the delete before its tombstone goes. The number that matters is the outage against gc_grace_seconds, not the replication factor.

options.text: Repair every node inside the grace, wipe and re-copy a node that was off longer, and alert before then.
options.part2: Ingleby kept the Monday repair on every node, well inside the 10-day grace, and added an alert for any computer off for 5 days, half the grace. The rule went on the crawl-space hatch: off longer than the grace, the computer is wiped and re-copied from the others, never just switched on. The next winter the cottage was off for 12 days, and the alert went off on the fifth. On the second night a guest burned her letter, and on the twelfth day at 03:00 the full compaction dropped the letter and its tombstone on the house and the barn, as before. At 09:00 Ingleby wiped the cottage's disk and it streamed its data from the other two, which held nothing for the letter. The Monday repair found three copies that matched, and the letter stayed burned: 0 bytes of it left on any disk. Bringing the cottage back took most of a morning instead of a minute.
options.senior: A tombstone is a promise with a deadline: every replica must hear about the delete before gc_grace_seconds runs out, so repair every node inside that window, with slack; the Cassandra docs suggest at least every 7 days for the default 10. A node that was off longer than the grace may hold data whose tombstones are gone everywhere else, so treat it as dead: wipe it, let it stream from the others, then repair. Alert well before the deadline. The cost is a slower return, and a routine someone must keep.

options.text: Never delete: mark each letter burned and hide it, so no copy anywhere holds a letter that can return.
options.part2: Ingleby changed Burn to set burned = true and had the app hide burned letters. The next winter the cottage was off for 12 days, and on the second night a guest burned her letter. The house and the barn wrote the flag; the cottage, off, kept the letter unflagged. When it came back, the Monday repair carried the flag to it, newer than the letter, and the letter stayed hidden everywhere. Nothing came back. But nothing went, either: three copies of her words, 6,936 bytes for a letter Isaura's size, sat on the disks under a flag, and would until someone deleted them for real. When the guest wrote to ask whether her letter was really gone, the warden couldn't say yes.
options.senior: A soft delete never returns, because an update with a newer timestamp beats an older value everywhere it lands. But it isn't a delete: the words stay on every disk and in every backup, so a promise of erasure, or a legal duty to erase, isn't met. Use it for an undo window, then delete for real, which still needs repair inside the grace.

sim.title: Replay the burned letter at Hollinmere
sim.lede: You're the warden with Ingleby's printout, replaying from 3 Feb 08:00. Isaura's letter, 2,312 bytes, written 1 Feb 21:15, sits on all three nodes, in each node's big, old SSTable. The cottage goes off at 09:00; at 12:00 it passes the 3 h max_hint_window, so no hints are kept for it after that. Isaura burns the letter at 22:10 on 4 Feb with a DELETE at QUORUM. Every write a node receives lands in a new, small SSTable. A nightly compaction at 03:00 merges a node's small SSTables only; a full compaction merges all of them, every 12 days, on 15 Feb and 27 Feb. In a merge, a letter older than a tombstone is dropped, and the tombstone itself goes only if it's older than gc_grace_seconds and no older copy of the letter sits on that node outside the merge. The repair runs Mondays at 02:00 among the nodes that are on, and gives every node every value another holds. A QUORUM read takes the first nodes to answer: the house, the barn, then the dairy and the stable if they exist, and last the cottage, whose link is slowest. Change the grace, the outage, the replication factor (5 adds the dairy and the stable), what happens when the cottage returns, or turn on soft delete, where Burn sets a burned flag instead. Changing a setting replays from 3 Feb 08:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next event to walk the story: tombstones on the house and the barn at 22:10 on 4 Feb, the 9 Feb repair without the cottage, both dropped at 15 Feb 03:00 (the tombstone 10 d 4 h 50 min old), the cottage back at 09:00, and the letter back at 16 Feb 02:00. Run to the end: 6,936 bytes on disk. Set the grace to 0: back at 16 Feb 02:00 all the same. Replication factor 5: back at 16 Feb 02:00, with 11,560 bytes. A 14-day grace: nothing comes back; now make the outage 20 days, and it is back at 2 Mar 02:00. Set the return to rebuild, which wipes the cottage and re-copies it from the others: nothing comes back, 0 bytes. Try a 5-day outage with the default grace. Soft delete: hidden, never back, and 6,936 bytes for good.

explain.oneLine: Nothing came back from the dead. The cottage was off when the letter was burned, so it never got the tombstone; ten days later compaction on the house and the barn dropped the letter and its tombstone, and the next repair, finding a letter on one node and nothing on two, copied the letter back.

steps.title: Two ways to keep data on disk.
steps.text: A storage engine is the part of a database that keeps rows on disk. A B-tree engine, like PostgreSQL's or InnoDB's, keeps each row on one page of a tree (case 1's pages) and changes that page, after logging the change first (case 4). A delete there doesn't erase on the spot either: PostgreSQL marks the old tuple dead and VACUUM reclaims the space later, and InnoDB delete-marks the record and a purge removes it. What matters here is that no older copy of the row is left behind in a file that never changes. An LSM tree, the design under Cassandra, works the other way round. A write goes to the commit log, its write-ahead log, and into the memtable in memory. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to disk as a new SSTable, sorted and immutable: never edited again. So a delete is a write too, a tombstone, and the old copy stays in its SSTable until a compaction merges it with that tombstone.

steps.title: Compaction, and what it costs.
steps.text: Compaction merges several SSTables into one, keeps the newest version of each value, and drops values hidden by a newer tombstone, plus tombstones old enough to go. Without it, reads would slow down and the disk would fill. The costs come in three kinds, usually called amplification. Write amplification: each value is rewritten several times as it is merged into bigger files. Read amplification: one read may have to check several SSTables for the same row; Bloom filters let it skip most files that can't hold the key (case 14 covers them). Space amplification: old versions and tombstones take disk until a merge removes them. Size-tiered compaction merges SSTables of similar size, cheap on writes. Leveled compaction keeps small SSTables in levels that don't overlap, more merging but fewer files per read. Cassandra lets you pick one per table.

steps.title: A tombstone has a deadline.
steps.text: A delete has to reach every replica: at once, through a hint kept for a node that is briefly off, through read repair, or through repair. The tombstone is what repair carries. If it is dropped before a replica hears of it, that replica's old copy looks like data the others lost. So each table has gc_grace_seconds, 864,000 by default, ten days, and the Cassandra docs give two conditions for dropping a tombstone: it must be older than gc_grace_seconds, and every SSTable holding older data for that row must be in the same compaction. Hints don't cover a long outage: no new hints are made once a node has been off longer than max_hint_window, 3h by default. That leaves repair, which the docs say should run on every node often enough that the grace never expires on unrepaired data.

steps.title: What happened under the floor.
steps.text: The cottage went off at 09:00 on 3 February, and three hours later the others stopped keeping hints for it. Isaura burned her letter at 22:10 on 4 February, 37 h 10 min into the outage: the DELETE at QUORUM succeeded on the house and the barn, two of three, and no hint was kept for the cottage. Each night's compaction merged only small, new SSTables, which held the tombstone but not the letter's old SSTable, so the tombstone stayed. At 03:00 on 15 February the full compaction merged everything on the house and the barn. The tombstone was 10 d 4 h 50 min old, past the 10-day grace, and the letter was in the same merge: both conditions held, and both went. Six hours later the cottage came back with the letter. At 02:00 on Monday the repair compared copies: a letter on one node, nothing on two. An absent row is not a vote; a value beats nothing, and the letter was streamed back.

steps.title: Tombstones also slow reads.
steps.text: Until compaction drops them, tombstones are read like rows. A read that scans a partition full of deleted rows has to hold every tombstone it meets in memory, so cassandra.yaml has two limits: tombstone_warn_threshold, 1,000 by default, which logs a warning, and tombstone_failure_threshold, 100,000, which aborts the query. That is the real cost behind the commenter's "tombstones are clutter", and the answer is usually a data model that deletes less, not a shorter grace.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next storm. A repair box at the top runs on every node inside the 10-day grace and points to the house, barn and cottage nodes. The house and barn keep tombstones until they are 10 days old. The cottage, off 12 days, is wiped and re-copied: an arrow from the barn to the cottage is labeled stream. Below the cottage an alert box fires when a node has been off 5 days.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next storm. Repair reaches every node inside the 10-day grace, so a tombstone always arrives before it may be dropped. A node off longer than the grace, like the cottage after 12 days, is wiped and re-copied from the others, then repaired, so the old letter on its disk never meets a cluster that has forgotten the burn. The alert fires at 5 days, half the grace.

fix.title: The fix: repair inside the grace, rebuild after it, and alert before it
fix.text: Run repair on every node more often than gc_grace_seconds, with slack: with the default 10 days, Hollinmere's Monday run already does it, as long as every node takes part. Watch outages against the grace. Alert when a node has been off for half of it, so there is time to bring it back and repair. If a node has been off longer than the grace, don't switch it back on as it was: wipe its data and let it stream from the other replicas, the way Cassandra replaces a dead node, then repair. Its old disk may hold letters whose tombstones are gone everywhere else. Keep gc_grace_seconds at the default unless you can prove your repairs always finish well inside a shorter one.

limits: Repair costs disk and network I/O, and Cassandra doesn't run it by itself; someone has to schedule it, watch that every run finishes on every node, and notice when one silently skips a node that is off, as the 9 February run did.
Rebuilding is slow, and while the node streams the cluster leans on fewer full copies; with replication factor 3, losing a second node in that window leaves QUORUM unreachable.
A long grace keeps tombstones longer, so a table with heavy deletes uses more disk and reads more tombstones; the fix for that is fewer deletes in the data model, not a shorter grace.

explain.seniorTake: An LSM tree buys fast, sequential writes by never editing a file, and pays in compaction, read amplification and deletes that are really writes. In a replicated LSM store, a delete is only finished when every replica has the tombstone, and the tombstone has a deadline. Treat gc_grace_seconds as a contract with your operations: repair every node inside it, alert before an outage reaches it, and wipe and rebuild a node that outlived it. Never shorten it to tidy the disks, and never take more replicas for a fix; nothing doesn't outvote anything. When the data is personal, check backups and soft-deleted rows too, because erasure means every copy.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: a delete is an insertion
realWorld.text: The Cassandra docs say "Cassandra treats a deletion as an insertion, and inserts a time-stamped deletion marker called a tombstone." The tombstones go through the write path into SSTables, and once one exists, queries ignore all values time-stamped before it.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: zombies and the grace period
realWorld.text: The same page sets gc_grace_seconds' default at 864000 seconds (ten days) and names the case: "If a node remains down or disconnected for longer than gc_grace_seconds, its deleted data will be repaired back to the other nodes and reappear in the cluster." It calls such data a zombie.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: two conditions to drop a tombstone
realWorld.text: "The tombstone must be older than gc_grace_seconds", and the SSTable holding it, plus all SSTables holding older data for the same partition, "must be included in the same compaction." The page adds that tombstones "will not be removed until a compaction event even if gc_grace_seconds has elapsed."

realWorld.title: Cassandra: the hint window
realWorld.text: cassandra.yaml's max_hint_window "defines the maximum amount of time a dead host will have hints generated", default 3h; after that, no new hints are made until the node has been seen alive and gone down again. Older versions named the key max_hint_window_in_ms, and the Hints page's prose still uses the old form.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: repair inside the grace
realWorld.text: The Repair page calls hints "a best effort" and says "repair should be run often enough that the gc grace period never expires on unrepaired data. Otherwise, deleted data could reappear." With the default 10 days, "repairing every node in your cluster at least once every 7 days will prevent this, while providing enough slack to allow for delays."

realWorld.title: DataStax (Cassandra 2.1 docs): wipe and bootstrap
realWorld.text: DataStax's older Cassandra 2.1 page on deletes says a node down longer than the grace can miss the delete, and that if the node doesn't come back within gc_grace_seconds, "remove the node, wipe it, and bootstrap it again."

realWorld.title: Cassandra today: replacing a dead node
realWorld.text: The current Apache docs replace a dead node by starting a new one with the replace_address_first_boot flag, which streams the data from the rest of the cluster, and say you "MUST run repair" afterwards if the node was down longer than max_hint_window before being replaced.

realWorld.title: Cassandra's storage engine
realWorld.text: "The core storage engine consists of memtables for in-memory data and immutable SSTables (Sorted String Tables) on disk," with a write-ahead log "referred to as the commit log". "SSTables are immutable, and never written to again after the memtable is flushed." The page warns: "Every write of data in Cassandra is re-written multiple times, known as write amplification." It adds that Bloom filters help reads.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: compaction strategies
realWorld.text: Size Tiered (STCS) "is the default compaction strategy, because it is useful as a fallback"; Leveled (LCS) "is optimized for read heavy workloads, or workloads with lots of updates and deletes"; and Unified (UCS) "is recommended for new workloads".

realWorld.title: Cassandra: tombstones slow reads
realWorld.text: cassandra.yaml explains that a scan keeps the tombstones it sees in memory, and says: "With workloads that generate a lot of tombstones, this can cause performance problems and even exhaust the server heap." tombstone_warn_threshold defaults to 1000 and tombstone_failure_threshold to 100000.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: the old version stays until VACUUM
realWorld.text: "In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version of the row." VACUUM later "removes dead row versions in tables and indexes and marks the space available for future reuse."

realWorld.title: InnoDB: delete-marked, then purged
realWorld.text: In InnoDB "a row is not physically removed from the database immediately when you delete it with an SQL statement"; it is removed later: "This removal operation is called a purge."

realWorld.title: The LSM-tree paper, 1996
realWorld.text: Patrick O'Neil, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick and Elizabeth O'Neil, "The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)", Acta Informatica, 1996: the design that batches changes in memory and merges them into larger sorted runs on disk.

realWorld.title: The B-tree paper, 1972
realWorld.text: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight, "Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indices", 1972: the paper behind the B-tree that most relational databases still use for tables and indexes.

realWorld.title: Bigtable, OSDI 2006
realWorld.text: Fay Chang, Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat and colleagues at Google, "Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data", OSDI 2006: the paper that made the memtable and the SSTable common names, and an ancestor of Cassandra's storage engine.

asked: B-tree or LSM tree: which would you choose and why?
What is compaction and what does it cost?
How can deleted data come back in a distributed database?
interview.answer: Start from the workload. A B-tree keeps each row on one page and changes it there, after logging; reads are predictable, often one path from the root to a leaf, and it suits read-heavy tables with point lookups and range scans. Its writes land on random pages, and page splits and cleanup such as VACUUM or purge add work. An LSM tree appends writes to a commit log and a memtable and flushes them as sorted, immutable SSTables, so writes are sequential and cheap, which suits heavy write streams. The bill is compaction: background merging that rewrites data several times (write amplification), reads that may check several SSTables (read amplification, eased by Bloom filters), and old versions and tombstones taking disk until merged (space amplification). Size-tiered compaction favours writes; leveled favours reads. Deleted data comes back when a replica misses a delete and the tombstone is dropped elsewhere before repair carries it over: compaction drops it once it's older than gc_grace_seconds, ten days by default in Cassandra, and repair then sees a value on one replica and nothing on the others and copies the value back. Prevent it by repairing every node inside the grace, alerting on long outages, and wiping and rebuilding a node that was down longer than the grace. Don't set the grace to zero, and don't expect more replicas to outvote it.

terms.def: A place where people who have lost someone stay for a while, away from home, to grieve with support. Hollinmere is one, in an old farmhouse.
The person who looks after a building overnight: doors, heating, and here the retreat's three computers.
The retreat's app where guests write letters to people they have lost. Its data lives in a three-node Cassandra cluster.
The button a guest presses on her last night to destroy a letter. It sends a DELETE for the letter at QUORUM.
The low gap between a house's ground floor and the earth, among its foundations. The cottage's computer sits there.
The part of a database that decides how rows are laid out on disk, written, found and removed. B-tree engines and LSM trees are the two common designs.
A storage engine that keeps rows in the pages of a B-tree and changes the page that holds a row, after logging the change. PostgreSQL and InnoDB work this way.
Log-structured merge tree: a storage engine that collects writes in memory, writes them out as sorted files that never change, and merges those files in the background. Cassandra uses one.
Cassandra's write-ahead log: every write is appended to it on disk first, so a crash can't lose writes still in the memtable.
An LSM tree's sorted table of recent writes in memory. When it fills, it is flushed to disk as a new SSTable.
Sorted String Table: one of Cassandra's data files on disk, sorted by key and written once from a memtable or a merge. It is never edited after.
Never changed once written. An SSTable is immutable, so a delete can't remove a row from it; only a merge into a new file can leave the row out.
A marker written by a delete in Cassandra that says a value was deleted at a given time. Older values it covers are hidden from reads until compaction removes them.
Merging several SSTables into one: keeping the newest version of each value, dropping values a tombstone hides, and dropping tombstones old enough to go.
In the sim, the 03:00 merge of a node's small, new SSTables only. It never includes the big, old SSTable that holds the letter.
In the sim, a merge of every SSTable on a node, every 12 days at 03:00: 3 Feb (before the sim opens), 15 Feb and 27 Feb.
A Cassandra table setting: how long a tombstone must be kept before compaction may drop it. The default is 864,000 seconds, ten days.
The time set by gc_grace_seconds during which a tombstone is kept, so that repair can carry it to every replica.
The Cassandra docs' word for deleted data that comes back: a replica that missed the delete still holds it after the tombstone is gone elsewhere, and repair copies it back.
A note a Cassandra node keeps of a write meant for a replica that is off, to hand over when it returns. Part of hinted handoff.
The cassandra.yaml setting for how long after a node goes down the others keep making hints for it. The default is 3h. Older versions called it max_hint_window_in_ms.
Copying data between nodes in bulk, as repair does for the parts of two replicas that differ, or as a new node does to fill its disk.
One stored value on a node with its timestamp: the letter, its tombstone or its burned flag.
Wiping a node's data and filling it again by streaming from the other replicas, instead of switching it back on with its old disk. Cassandra's form is replacing a dead node.
The Cassandra startup flag that makes a new node take a dead node's place and stream its data from the rest of the cluster.
A new Cassandra node joining the cluster and streaming the data it will hold from the other nodes before it serves reads.
A replica holding nothing for a row. Repair and reads treat it as nothing to compare, not as a vote for deleted, so any value beats it.
One read having to look in several places, such as several SSTables, for one row.
Disk used beyond the live data: old versions and tombstones kept until a merge removes them.
A small summary of the keys a file holds that can answer definitely not here or maybe, so a read skips most files. Case 14 covers it.
A compaction strategy that merges SSTables of similar size. Cheap on writes; a row may sit in several files. Cassandra's default.
A compaction strategy that keeps small SSTables in levels that don't overlap. More merging, fewer files per read; suits read-heavy tables and many updates or deletes.
A newer Cassandra compaction strategy designed to cover many workloads; the docs recommend it for new ones.
PostgreSQL's cleanup command: it removes dead row versions from tables and indexes and marks the space for reuse.
In PostgreSQL, an old copy of a row left on its page by an UPDATE or DELETE, kept while other transactions may still see it, until VACUUM removes it.
InnoDB's first step for a delete: the record is marked deleted where it sits, and removed later by a purge.
InnoDB's background removal of delete-marked rows and their index records, once no transaction needs the old version.
Marking a row deleted, for example with a burned flag, and hiding it in the app, instead of deleting it. The data stays on disk.
A B-tree page that is full being split into two to make room for a new entry, which also changes the page above it.
The memory Cassandra's Java process keeps its working objects in. A scan that holds too many tombstones there can run it out.
Cassandra's statement for changing values in a row. Each changed value gets a new timestamp, so it beats older copies.
With soft delete on, the value Burn writes instead of a tombstone: burned = true. The letter's words stay beside it.
In the sim, a read answered by the first two of three nodes, or three of five: house, barn, then dairy and stable, and last the cottage, whose link is slowest.
2,312 bytes for each copy of Isaura's letter held on any node's disk, hidden or not, counting a node that is off.
The two extra computers that replication factor 5 adds, in the farm's dairy and stable.
A cassandra.yaml limit: a read that scans more tombstones than this logs a warning. The default is 1,000.
A cassandra.yaml limit: a read that scans more tombstones than this is aborted. The default is 100,000.
An app saving a draft by itself every few seconds while someone writes.
The GDPR article that lets a data subject have personal data erased by the controller without undue delay, on grounds the article lists.
A computer science journal published by Springer, where both the B-tree paper (1972) and the LSM-tree paper (1996) appeared.
USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation, a conference where Google published Bigtable in 2006.
Google's storage system for structured data, described in a 2006 paper. Its memtables and SSTables shaped Cassandra's engine.

atWork: Picture a common incident: a customer asks for their account to be deleted, the request succeeds, and weeks later support finds the profile live again. A node had been off for longer than the grace, and when it came back, repair copied the deleted rows back. Look for the same in your own systems. With read-only access, list every store that keeps replicas and deletes with tombstones: Cassandra, ScyllaDB, and any LSM-based store. For each table, note gc_grace_seconds and when each node last finished a repair, and check that repair reaches every node inside the grace with room to spare; a run that silently skips a node that is off counts for nothing. Find your runbook for a node that comes back after a long outage: does it say to wipe and rebuild a node that was off longer than the grace, or just to switch it on? Check that an alert fires well before an outage reaches the grace. Look for soft-deleted rows and backups that still hold data your app calls deleted. If personal data is involved and the GDPR applies, Article 17, the right to erasure, expects the controller to erase it without undue delay when a valid request arrives, so a deletion that can come back from a replica, a soft-deleted row or a backup is a gap to close. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.10 (information deletion) expects information to be deleted when no longer needed, so write down how a delete reaches every replica, the repair schedule and the rebuild rule, and keep their logs as evidence. Build both into the first version of the table, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company keeps customer profiles in a Cassandra table with replication factor 3 and the default gc_grace_seconds. One node was offline for 13 days for a disk swap. During that time a customer asked for account deletion, and the DELETE at QUORUM succeeded. A week after the node was switched back on, the profile is visible again. Explain how, and what you would change.

keyIdeas.idea: The offline node missed the delete and kept the profile, with no hint kept for it because it had been off longer than the hint window
Compaction on the other nodes dropped the profile and its tombstone once the tombstone was older than gc_grace_seconds, ten days
Repair found the profile on one node and nothing on the others and copied it back, because an absent row is not a vote
Repair every node inside the grace, alert on long outages, and wipe and rebuild a node that was off longer than the grace

recall.model: The node that was offline never got the tombstone. The DELETE succeeded on the other two replicas, which wrote tombstones, but the third had been off for days, far longer than the 3h hint window, so no hint was kept for it and it still held the profile. Ten days later, once the tombstones were older than gc_grace_seconds, compaction on the two live nodes merged each tombstone with the profile it hid and dropped both. When the third node came back after 13 days, the next repair found the profile on one replica and nothing on the other two. An absent row is not a vote, so repair copied it back to both, and it reappeared: a zombie. I'd repair every node inside the grace with slack, alert when a node has been off for half the grace, and never switch on a node that was off longer than the grace: wipe it and rebuild it by streaming from the other replicas, then repair. I'd leave the grace at the default and check backups for the deleted profile too.

recall.prompt: A tombstone in a Cassandra table is now older than gc_grace_seconds. When can compaction drop it?
options: In any compaction on that node, as soon as the grace has passed
Only in a compaction that also includes every SSTable on that node holding older data for the same row
Only after every replica has acknowledged the tombstone to the coordinator
Never: tombstones stay until the table itself is dropped
recall.why: The Cassandra docs give two conditions: the tombstone must be older than gc_grace_seconds, and the SSTables holding older data for the same partition must be in the same compaction. Otherwise the older copy would reappear once its tombstone was gone. At Hollinmere the nightly merges never included the letter's old SSTable, so the tombstone survived them, and both went together in the full compaction on 15 February.

recall.prompt: In a design interview you're asked to choose a storage engine for two tables: a sensor feed taking 40,000 small writes a second, read mostly as recent ranges, and a customer accounts table read by id far more often than it's written. Which kind of engine would you lean towards for each, and what does each choice cost?

keyIdeas.idea: An LSM tree for the write-heavy feed: writes are appended to a log and a memtable and flushed in sorted batches, so they are sequential and cheap
The LSM tree's bill: background merging rewrites data (write amplification) and reads may check several SSTables (read amplification), helped by Bloom filters
A B-tree for the read-heavy accounts table: each row lives on one page, so reads by id are predictable; writes cost random page changes

recall.model: I'd lean towards an LSM tree for the sensor feed. Each write is appended to the commit log and put in the memtable, which is flushed as a sorted, immutable SSTable, so writes are sequential and cheap, and recent ranges come out sorted. The cost is compaction: background merging rewrites each value several times, which is write amplification, and until files are merged a read may check several SSTables, which is read amplification, eased by Bloom filters. Old versions and deletes also take disk until merged. For the accounts table I'd lean towards a B-tree. Each row lives on one page, so a lookup by id is a predictable walk from the root to a leaf, and there is only one place to check. Its cost is on writes: they change random pages, pages split as they fill, and cleanup such as VACUUM runs later. At 40,000 writes a second that cost would hurt; for a read-heavy table it barely shows.

recall.prompt: A query reads a Cassandra partition holding many deleted rows. With the default cassandra.yaml, after how many scanned tombstones is the query aborted?
recall.why: tombstone_failure_threshold defaults to 100,000: a read that scans more tombstones than that is aborted. tombstone_warn_threshold, 1,000 by default, only logs a warning. A scan has to keep the tombstones it meets in memory so it can pass them to the coordinator, which is why cassandra.yaml says heavy tombstone workloads can even exhaust the heap.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The hatch rule works. In June the barn computer's power supply failed and it was off for 11 days; Ingleby wiped it and re-copied it before switching it on, and nothing came back. But the journal now has autosave: every 2 seconds while a guest writes, the app inserts a new draft row for her letter and deletes the previous one. A guest who writes three hours a day makes about 5,400 deletes a day. On her first evening the log began warning about the tombstones her journal page was reading. On day 19 of her stay the page stopped opening at all; the log said the read gave up after more than 100,000 tombstones. Ingleby wants to set gc_grace_seconds to 0 on the drafts table, just for drafts.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does her journal page slow down and then fail, and what should Ingleby do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Every autosave's delete writes a tombstone that reads must scan past until compaction drops it; Cassandra warns at 1,000 and aborts at 100,000
Stop deleting: keep one draft row per letter and overwrite it, so an autosave is an update, not an insert plus a delete
Don't use a zero grace: drafts are replicated too, and a node that missed deletes would bring them back; keep the grace and repair inside it

coldCase.model: Each autosave is an insert plus a delete, and every delete writes a tombstone. Until compaction drops them, at least ten days later, a read of her drafts still has to read past every one, holding them in memory: past 1,000 Cassandra logs a warning, which is tombstone_warn_threshold, and past 100,000 it aborts the read, the failure threshold. So stop deleting. Keep one draft row per letter and overwrite it on each autosave; an update with a newer timestamp simply replaces the old value, and no tombstone is written. When the letter is finished or burned, that one row is deleted once. Don't set the grace to zero, not even for drafts: they are replicated like the letters, and the first node that is off during a delete would make old drafts reappear after the next merge, the zombie problem from February. Keep the grace at the default and the repair inside it.
